'''Lynne Quarmby''' is a [[Canadians|Canadian]] scientist, activist, and politician. She is a professor in the Department of Molecular Biology and Biochemistry<ref name="SFU MBB Faculty Page">{{cite web|title=Lynne Quarmby|url=https://www.sfu.ca/mbb/people/faculty/lynne-quarmby.html |website=SFU Dept. of Molecular Biology and Biochemistry}}</ref> at [[Simon Fraser University]] in [[Burnaby]], [[British Columbia]]. She was a candidate for the [[Green Party of Canada]] in [[Burnaby North—Seymour]] in the [[42nd Canadian federal election|2015 federal election]],<ref name=Nomination>{{cite news|title=Lynne Quarmby elected Green Party Candidate in Burnaby North-Seymour|url=http://www.vancouverobserver.com/news/lynne-quarmby-elected-green-party-candidate-burnaby-north-seymour|accessdate=26 February 2015|work=Vancouver Observer|date=14 January 2015}}</ref> and is the Green Party of Canada's Science Policy Critic.<ref name="Science Policy Critic">{{cite news|title=Elizabeth May Appoints Green Candidate Lynne Quarmby as Science Policy Critic|url=https://greenparty.ca/en/media-release/2015-01-23/elizabeth-may-appoints-green-candidate-lynne-quarmby-science-policy-critic|accessdate=24 February 2015|work=Green Party of Canada|date=23 January 2015}}</ref>

==Research and education==
Quarmby completed a BSc in [[Marine Biology]] and a MSc in Biological [[Oceanography]] at the [[University of British Columbia]] before moving to the [[University of Connecticut]] to complete her PhD in [[Biochemistry]].<ref name="SFU MBB Faculty Page" /> She worked as a [[postdoctoral fellow]] in the lab of [[Nobel laureate]] [[Alfred G. Gilman|Alfred Gilman]]  at the [[University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center]] in [[Austin, Texas|Austin]], TX, then in the lab of Criss Hartzell at [[Emory University]] in [[Atlanta]], GA, where she also held her first faculty position.<ref name="ASCB Member Profile">{{cite news|title=Lynne Quarmby|url=https://quarmby.ca/wp-content/uploads/ASCB-profile.pdf|accessdate=26 February 2015|work=ASCB Newsletter|date=September 2006}}</ref> She moved her lab to Simon Fraser University in 2000.

Quarmby's research has been aimed at understanding the signals and mechanisms of deflagellation, the process by which cells shed their [[cilia]] into the environment.<ref name="Cellular deflagellation">{{cite book|last1=Quarmby|first1=Lynne M.|chapter=Cellular deflagellation|volume=233|pages=47–91|doi=10.1016/S0074-7696(04)33002-0|pmid=15037362|title=International Review of Cytology|date=2004 |isbn=978-0-12-364637-8 }}</ref> Cilia are found on most [[eukaryotic cells]] and on most cells in the human body, and defects in a cell's ability to form or maintain its cilia can cause diseases known as [[ciliopathies]], that may include symptoms such as [[cystic kidney disease]], [[blindness]], and [[obesity]].<ref name=Ciliopathies>{{cite news|last1=Krisch|first1=Joshua A.|title=Why Scientists Are Blaming Cilia for Human Disease|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-scientists-are-blaming-cilia-for-human-disease/|accessdate=17 February 2015|work=Scientific American|date=10 December 2014}}</ref> Through her research using the single-celled ciliated green alga [[Chlamydomonas reinhardtii]] as a model organism, Quarmby identified members of the NIMA-related family of [[serine/threonine kinases]] that function in deflagellation<ref name="Deflagellation Genetics">{{cite journal|last1=Finst|first1=Rip J.|last2=Kim|first2=Peter J.|last3=Quarmby|first3=Lynne M.|title=Genetics of the deflagellation pathway in Chlamydomonas|journal=Genetics|date=1998|volume=149|issue=2|pages=927–936|doi=10.1093/genetics/149.2.927|pmid=9611203|pmc=1460167}}</ref><ref name="FA2 Deflagellation">{{cite journal|last1=Mahjoub|first1=Moe R.|last2=Montpetit|first2=Ben|last3=Zhao|first3=Lifan|last4=Finst|first4=Rip J.|last5=Goh|first5=Benjamin|last6=Kim|first6=Apollos C.|last7=Quarmby|first7=Lynne M.|title=The FA2 gene of Chlamydomonas encodes a NIMA family kinase with roles in cell cycle progression and microtubule severing during deflagellation|journal=J Cell Sci|date=2002|volume=115|issue=Pt 8|pages=1759–1768|doi=10.1242/jcs.115.8.1759|pmid=11950892|url=http://jcs.biologists.org/content/115/8/1759.long|accessdate=17 February 2015|url-access=subscription}}</ref> as well as in the assembly and maintenance of cilia.<ref name="Science Daily CNK2">{{cite news|title=Cellular tail length tells human disease tale|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/10/131031124920.htm|accessdate=26 February 2015|work=Science Daily|date=31 October 2013}}</ref><ref name="Quarmby NEKs">{{cite journal|title=
 [Demonstration of tumor inhibiting properties of a strongly immunostimulating low-molecular weight substance. Comparative studies with ifosfamide on the immuno-labile DS carcinosarcoma. Stimulation of the autoimmune activity for approx. 20 days by BA 1, a N-(2-cyanoethylene)-urea. Novel prophylactic possibilities] 
|journal=Arzneimittel-Forschung|volume=25|issue=9|pages=1369–79|pmid=22|year=1975|last1=Ardenne|first1=M.|last2=Reitnauer|first2=P. G.}}</ref> Her group went on to show that [[NEK8]] localizes to cilia,<ref name="NEK Localization">{{cite journal|last1=Mahjoub|first1=Moe R.|last2=Trapp|first2=Melissa L.|last3=Quarmby|first3=Lynne M.|title=NIMA-related kinases defective in murine models of polycystic kidney diseases localize to primary cilia and centrosomes|journal=J Am Soc Nephrol|date=2005|volume=16|issue=12|pages=3485–3489|pmid=16267153|url=http://jasn.asnjournals.org/content/16/12/3485.long|accessdate=17 February 2015|doi=10.1681/asn.2005080824|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and that mutations in NEK8 interfere with its ciliary localization<ref name="Nek8 Cystogenesis">{{cite journal|last1=Trapp|first1=Melissa L.|last2=Galtseva|first2=Alevtina|last3=Manning|first3=Danielle K.|last4=Beier|first4=David R.|last5=Rosenblum|first5=Norman D.|last6=Quarmby|first6=Lynne M.|title=Defects in ciliary localization of Nek8 is associated with cystogenesis|journal=Pediatr Nephrol|date=2008|volume=23|issue=3|pages=377–387|doi=10.1007/s00467-007-0692-y|pmid=18189147|pmc=6890203}}</ref> and cause a severe juvenile cystic kidney disease known as [[nephronophthisis]],<ref name="Human NEK8">{{cite journal|last1=Otto|first1=Edgar A.|last2=Trapp|first2=Melissa L.|last3=Schultheiss|first3=Ulla T.|last4=Helou|first4=Juliana|last5=Quarmby|first5=Lynne M.|last6=Hildebrandt|first6=Friedhelm|authorlink6=Friedhelm Hildebrandt|title=NEK8 Mutations Affect Ciliary and Centrosomal Localization and May Cause Nephronophthisis|journal=J Am Soc Nephrol|date=2008|volume=19|issue=3|pages=587–592|doi=10.1681/ASN.2007040490|pmid=18199800|url=http://jasn.asnjournals.org/content/19/3/587.long|accessdate=17 February 2015|pmc=2391043}}</ref> underscoring the important link between cilia and cystic kidney disease.

Quarmby's work has been funded by the [[Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada]] (NSERC), the [[Canadian Institutes for Health Research]] (CIHR), and the [[Kidney Foundation of Canada]] (KFoC).<ref name="NSERC Funding">{{cite journal|url=http://www.nserc-crsng.gc.ca/NSERC-CRSNG/FundingDecisions-DecisionsFinancement/ResearchGrants-SubventionsDeRecherche/ResultsInsDetail-ResultatsEtabDetails_eng.asp?Year=2011&Institution=63|last=NSERC-CRSNG|title=2011 Research Grants Competition - Results by Institution|journal=Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada|accessdate=26 February 2015}}</ref><ref name="CIHR Funding">{{cite web|url=http://webapps.cihr-irsc.gc.ca/funding/detail_e?pResearchId=4963865&p_version=CIHR&p_language=E&p_session_id=|website=Canadian Research Information System|accessdate=26 February 2015}}{{Dead link|date=July 2022 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref name="KFOC Funding">{{cite web|title=KFoC Supporting Research Excellence|url=http://www.kidney.ca/document.doc?id=83|accessdate=26 February 2015|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304002625/http://www.kidney.ca/document.doc?id=83|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2011 NSERC recognized Quarmby's research program by awarding her a Discovery Accelerator Supplement, a funding program reserved for researchers who show strong potential to become international leaders within their field.<ref name=DAS>{{cite web|title=Competition Results for the Discovery Accelerator Supplements Program 2011|url=http://www.nserc-crsng.gc.ca/NSERC-CRSNG/FundingDecisions-DecisionsFinancement/DiscoveryAcceleratorSupplements-SupplementsAccelerationDecouverte/index_eng.asp?Year=2011|website=NSERC-CRSNG|accessdate=26 February 2015}}</ref>

Quarmby is known for outstanding undergraduate teaching, and received a SFU Teaching Excellence Award in 2011.<ref name="Teaching Excellence">{{cite news|last1=Luckow|first1=Diane|title=2011 Teaching Excellence Awards|url=https://www.sfu.ca/sfunews/stories/2012/2011-teaching-excellence-awards.html|accessdate=17 February 2015|work=SFU News|date=16 February 2012}}</ref>

Quarmby was the co-recipient of the 2015 Nora and Ted Sterling Prize in Support of Controversy.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sfu.ca/sterlingprize/recipients/stephencollis-lynnequarmby.html|title=The Nora and Ted Sterling Prize in Support of Controversy|last=|first=|date=|website=|access-date=}}</ref>

==Personal life==

Quarmby lives in [[Burnaby]], British Columbia. She is a painter, and her science-inspired art has been featured in the magazine ''The Scientist''.<ref name=Art>{{cite news|last1=Bernstein|first1=Rachel|title=Bridging Two Worlds|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/39633/title/Bridging-Two-Worlds/|accessdate=26 February 2015|work=The Scientist|date=4 April 2014}}</ref> Her adult son, Jacob Sheehy, lives in [[Toronto]] Ontario, where he runs a company called [[PressureNET]].<ref>{{cite news |title=How your smartphone could help predict the weather |last=CBC |url=https://www.cbc.ca/radio/spark/273-school-bus-wi-fi-cuba-s-alternative-internet-capitalism-2-0-and-more-1.2928720/how-your-smartphone-could-help-predict-the-weather-1.2928788 |journal=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |date=25 January 2015}}</ref>

==Advocacy and politics==
In May 2010, Quarmby wrote an op-ed in the [[Ottawa Citizen]] on gender equality in Canadian science and technology, after the Canada Excellence Research Chairs program did not select any women scientists for the nineteen awards it handed out.<ref name=Op-ed>{{cite news|last1=Quarmby|first1=Lynne|title=Elite research needs more women|work=The Ottawa Citizen|date=8 June 2010}}</ref><ref name="CERC Gender Bias">{{cite news|last1=Steffenhagen|first1=Janet|title=Exclusion of women from prestigious university appointments reignites battle of the sexes|work=The Vancouver Sun|date=28 May 2010}}</ref> This prompted the Vancouver Sun to name her one of 100 BC "Women of Influence" in 2010.<ref name="Women of Influence">{{cite news|last1=Quarmby|first1=Lynne|title=Women of Influence: Science and Medicine|url=https://vancouversun.com/health/Women+influence+Science+medicine/3749854/story.html|accessdate=26 February 2015|work=The Vancouver Sun|date=29 October 2010}}</ref> She has been an active member of the [[American Society for Cell Biology]]'s Women in Cell Biology Committee throughout her career.<ref name="ASCB Member Profile"/>

Quarmby has maintained a blog called ''The Crux'' on which she has written on the process of science and the state of science funding in Canada, with guest posts on a variety of science and climate issues.<ref name="Introducing The Crux">{{cite web|last1=Quarmby|first1=Lynne|title=Introducing The Crux|url=http://blog.quarmby.ca/introducing-the-crux/|website=The Crux|accessdate=26 February 2015|archive-date=27 February 2015|archive-url=https://archive.today/20150227062707/http://blog.quarmby.ca/introducing-the-crux/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Her work has been featured on the literary blog ''Numero Cinq''.<ref name="Numero Cinq">{{cite web|last1=Quarmby|first1=Lynne|title=A Feeling for the Model Organism|url=http://numerocinqmagazine.com/?s=quarmby&searchsubmit=|website=Numero Cinq|accessdate=26 February 2015}}</ref>

More recently, Quarmby has been an advocate for action on [[climate change]]. In May 2012, she joined the group Voters Taking Action on Climate Change (VTACC)<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.vtacc.org/ | title=Voters Taking Action on Climate Change – Connecting the dots between fossil fuel exports and climate change | access-date=2015-02-27 | archive-date=2022-03-08 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220308110349/https://vtacc.org/ | url-status=dead }}</ref> in an anti-coal protest in which they blockaded a coal train carrying coal from [[Wyoming]] to [[Deltaport]] for export overseas.<ref>{{cite news |title=Anti-coal protesters arrested in White Rock |last=CBC News |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/anti-coal-protesters-arrested-in-white-rock-1.1210172 |journal=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |date=5 May 2012}}</ref> Thirteen protesters, including Quarmby, were arrested for trespassing under the Railway Safety Act.<ref name="Civil Disobedience Interview">{{cite news|last1=MacKinnon|first1=J.B.|title=I Broke the Law to Defeat Climate Change|url=https://thetyee.ca/News/2012/09/19/Whiterock-Blockade/|accessdate=26 February 2015|work=The Tyee|date=19 September 2012}}</ref> She was a featured speaker at the [[People's Climate March (2014)|People's Climate March]] in Vancouver, BC.<ref name="Ten things">{{cite news|last1=Quarmby|first1=Lynne|title=Ten things we can do to take action on Climate Change|url=http://commonground.ca/OLD/iss/279/cg279_tenthings.shtml|accessdate=26 February 2015|work=Common Ground|date=October 2014|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304132132/http://commonground.ca/OLD/iss/279/cg279_tenthings.shtml|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Climate March">{{cite news|last1=Quarmby|first1=Lynne|title=March for the Climate|url=https://vancouversun.com/technology/Opinion+March+climate/10215292/story.html|accessdate=26 February 2015|work=The Vancouver Sun|date=19 September 2014}}</ref>

In November 2014, while Quarmby was involved in the protests of the [[Kinder Morgan|Trans Mountain Oil Pipeline]], she was arrested for [[civil contempt]].<ref name=Cole>{{cite news |title=Lynne Quarmby launches Green campaign in Burnaby North-Seymour |last=Cole |first=Yolande |url=https://www.straight.com/news/812386/lynne-quarmby-launches-green-campaign-burnaby-north-seymour?comment_mode=1#add-new-comment |journal=[[The Georgia Straight]] |date=22 January 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=More arrests on Burnaby Mountain as Kinder Morgan moves in |last=Moreau |first=Jennifer |url=http://www.burnabynow.com/news/more-arrests-on-burnaby-mountain-as-kinder-morgan-moves-in-1.1616359# |journal=[[Burnaby Now]] |date=21 November 2014}}</ref> The charges were dismissed after it was discovered that she and other protestors had not actually crossed the line prohibited by the court because of a mix-up about GPS coordinates used in the relevant court order.<ref>{{cite news |title=Civil contempt charges dropped against B.C. pipeline protesters |last=Keller |first=James and [[The Canadian Press]] |url=https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/2014/11/27/civil_contempt_charges_dropped_against_bc_pipeline_protesters.html |journal=[[The Toronto Star]] |date=27 November 2014}}</ref>

In December 2014, Quarmby announced that she would be seeking the [[Green Party of Canada]] nomination in [[Burnaby North—Seymour]] for the [[42nd Canadian federal election|upcoming federal election]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Kinder Morgan arrestee Lynne Quarmby to run for Greens in federal election |last=Prystupa |first=Mychaylo |url=http://www.vancouverobserver.com/news/kinder-morgan-arrestee-lynne-quarmby-run-greens-federal-election |journal=[[Vancouver Observer]] |date=17 December 2014 |access-date=25 January 2015 |archive-date=23 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191023140609/https://www.vancouverobserver.com/news/kinder-morgan-arrestee-lynne-quarmby-run-greens-federal-election |url-status=dead }}</ref>  She was confirmed as the candidate in January 2015,<ref>{{cite news |title=Lynne Quarmby elected Green Party Candidate in Burnaby North-Seymour |last=Vancouver Observer |author-link=Vancouver Observer |url=http://www.vancouverobserver.com/news/lynne-quarmby-elected-green-party-candidate-burnaby-north-seymour |journal=[[Vancouver Observer]] |date=14 January 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=SFU's Quarmby to run for Greens in Burnaby North-Seymour |last=Chow |first=Wanda |url=http://www.burnabynewsleader.com/news/288604531.html |journal=[[Burnaby News Leader]] |date=14 January 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=SFU professor and activist acclaimed as Green candidate in Burnaby |last=Morton |first=Brian |url=https://vancouversun.com/technology/professor+activist+acclaimed+Green+candidate+Burnaby/10729329/story.html |journal=[[Vancouver Sun]] |date=19 January 2015}}</ref> and placed fourth, with five percent of the vote.<ref>{{cite news| title=Burnaby North-Seymour: Tech CEO's win a surprise | date = 20 October 2015 |url=https://vancouversun.com/news/burnaby+north+seymour+tech+surprise/11451177/story.html}}</ref>
